title: What change gives the three-arm figure three angles of symmetry?
description: The three-arm figure from the book has unequal gaps and only the full turn fits. The angles between its dotted lines are changed until the gaps are equal, and the size of each gap is worked out from the full turn. Keeko's doubt is that longer arms would be enough.
teaching_notes: One idea: the three angles between the dotted lines must be equal, and they share the full turn of three hundred sixty degrees. Watch for students who change the length of the arms instead of the gaps.

source: Can anything in the three-arm figure be changed to make it h
video_script.why: The child finds that the three gaps of a three-arm figure must be made equal for the figure to have three angles of symmetry.
video_script.substitution: the book's three-arm figure, with the angles between the dotted lines changed
video_script.anchor: the book's figure with three radial arms and dotted lines between them
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko makes the arms longer and thinks the figure gets three angles of symmetry.
video_script.payoff_line: Make all three angles equal, one hundred twenty degrees each

final_answer.value: Yes, make all three angles between adjacent dotted lines 120°
final_answer.spoken: yes, make all three angles between neighbouring dotted lines one hundred twenty degrees

hold_back: Yes, make all three angles between adjacent dotted lines 120°
maths_rules: the three-arm figure with unequal angles has only 360° as an angle of symmetry
to have 3 angles of symmetry the three angles between the dotted lines must be equal
the three angles share the full turn: 360 ÷ 3 = 120
longer arms leave the gaps where they were, so the turn still misses
video_script.design: The three-arm figure with dotted lines between the arms. The dotted lines are moved until the three angles are equal, and the angle is worked out. Keeko's doubt is that longer arms are enough.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; the three-arm figure with dotted lines between the arms and unequal gaps

marks.book: the title card From your book arrives
marks.fig: the three-arm figure appears with dotted lines between the arms

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book, about the three-arm figure.
<bookmark mark='fig'/>Only a full turn brings this figure back onto itself.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Can we change the angles between the dotted lines, to give it three angles of symmetry?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the figure with its dot; a curved arrow round the dot; the words angle of symmetry; the three angles between the dotted lines named first, second and third

marks.name: the words angle of symmetry appear beside the curved arrow
marks.abc: the three angles between the dotted lines are marked first, second and third

narration: <bookmark mark='name'/>A turn after which the figure looks the same is called an angle of symmetry.
<bookmark mark='abc'/>The dotted lines make three angles round the dot.
We call them the first, the second and the third angle.

beats.on_screen: Given: 3 radial arms; the 3 angles between the dotted lines are not equal
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the figure has three radial arms.
The three angles between the dotted lines are not equal.

beats.on_screen: To find: a change that gives 3 angles of symmetry
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find a change that gives three angles of symmetry.

beats.on_screen: turn the figure by one gap: the first angle lands on the second, the second on the third, the third on the first

marks.turn: the figure turns and the three angles move onto each other
marks.lands: the first angle lands on the second and the second on the third

narration: <bookmark mark='turn'/>Step one, a turned copy must overlap the figure.
<bookmark mark='lands'/>The first angle must land on the second, and the second on the third.
The third angle must land on the first.

beats.on_screen: first angle = second angle = third angle

marks.eq: the equals signs appear between the three angles

narration: <bookmark mark='eq'/>Step two, angles that land on each other must be the same size.
The three angles must be equal.

beats.on_screen: the three angles share the full turn: 360° ÷ 3 = 120° for each angle

marks.share: the three angles fill the circle round the dot

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>Step three, the three angles share the full turn of three hundred sixty degrees.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Three hundred sixty divided by three is one hundred twenty degrees for each angle.

beats.on_screen: Answer: Yes, make all three angles between adjacent dotted lines 120°
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Make all three angles equal, one hundred twenty degrees each.
Yes, that gives three angles of symmetry.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the figure
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a bubble from Keeko says longer arms; the arms stretch and the dotted lines stay where they were; the bubble is struck out

marks.long: the arms stretch while the dotted lines stay in place

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks we should make the arms longer.
<bookmark mark='long'/>Longer arms leave the gaps exactly where they were.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The gaps are still unequal, so the turn still misses.
